economics.government-analyse-1.0007.all: Private owner seeks profit: may cut costs/jobs, reduce pay or worsen conditions, cutting union power; but rising passenger numbers and private investment may expand airport, creating jobs, training, productivity-related pay; loss of job security vs state.

economics.growth-data.0009.b: Falling consumer spending lowers demand/revenue/profit; firms cut output, lay off workers, cut investment; high energy costs raise costs; some close; inferior/discount firms may gain.
economics.growth-data.0009.c: Recession reduces AD so demand-pull inflation falls; spare capacity, unemployment restrains wages. But high energy prices cause cost-push inflation (stagflation); depends on duration/severity, exchange rate, gov policy. Judgement: inflation likely eases but energy costs may keep it high short run.

economics.growth-diagram.0016.all: PPC shifts inward (left/down) parallel-ish to a new curve PPC1 inside original, both axes intercepts reduced; labelled PPC1.

economics.growth-explain.0002.all: Fast growth means AD rising faster than productive capacity; spare capacity used up, shortages of labour/resources bid up wages and costs; firms raise prices - demand-pull inflation.

economics.growth-mcq-def.0005.all: D - negative growth for two consecutive quarters

economics.inflation-analyse-1.0003.all: Cost-push: rising energy and food prices raise firms' costs, passed on as higher prices; wage-price spiral as workers demand higher wages, raising costs further; possibly demand-pull from higher incomes/spending.

economics.inflation-data.0017.b: Delayed purchases cut consumer spending, lowers demand/output, firms cut jobs, profits fall; real debt burden rises; deflationary spiral; exports more competitive.
economics.inflation-data.0017.c: Harmful: delayed spending, falling output, unemployment, real debt up. Not harmful: fall is small (1.6%), may be supply-side/benign (lower costs, tech), real incomes rise, exports competitive. Judgement depends on cause and persistence.

economics.intervention-pol-analyse-1.000.all: Fines raise cost of polluting above the limit, giving incentive to cut waste/invest in cleaner tech; internalise external cost. Permits cap total pollution (21% reduction), price on pollution, firms that cut cheaply sell permits - efficient reduction; cap tightened over time.

economics.intervention-pol-analyse-2.000.all: Ban reduces demand for older high-emission vehicles (price falls, some scrapped/sold elsewhere); grant lowers effective price of EVs, demand for EVs shifts right, higher sales/price; supply of EVs may increase; shift in market composition.

economics.intervention-pol-assess-1.0006.all: Permits: guaranteed cap 30%, market-based efficiency, revenue, incentive to innovate; but permit price volatile, hard to set allocation, monitoring. Fines: simple, but need enforcement, may be too low, no incentive below limit. Judgement depends on enforcement and fine level.

economics.intervention-pol-assess-2.0001.all: Regulation (ban) directly removes high-emission vehicles - certain effect, quick; but costly enforcement, hurts poorer drivers, may push traffic elsewhere. Alternatives: grant V$1,000 (small subsidy), congestion charge/tax, public transport. Judgement: combination best.

economics.intervention-pol-evaluate-1.00.all: As assess: permits guarantee 35% cut, efficient, innovation, revenue; drawbacks: allocation, price volatility, monitoring, few firms on one river - thin market. Fines: simple, cheaper to run; but fine level, enforcement, only punish after damage. Conclusion with conditions.

economics.intervention-pol-evaluate-2.00.all: Ban: direct, certain reduction in city-centre emissions; but enforcement cost, unfair on low income, displacement. Grant S£3,000 lowers EV cost but costly to gov, may subsidise those who would buy anyway. Alternatives: taxes, congestion charge, public transport. Judgement: regulation effective short-term, combination best.

economics.labour-analyse-1.0006.all: Employed low-paid workers gain higher income/living standards, motivation; but higher labour costs may cause small retail/hospitality firms to cut staff/hours, unemployment esp. young/unskilled; possible automation; depends on elasticity of demand for labour.

economics.labour-data.0018.b: Engineers: scarce skilled labour (low supply, long training), high demand/high MRP; shop assistants: plentiful supply of low-skilled labour, many applicants, so lower wage.
economics.labour-data.0018.c: May fall: training/education increases supply of engineers, migration, minimum wage raises low pay. May not: tech raises demand for engineers, automation lowers demand for shop workers, training barriers. Judgement: unlikely to fall much.

economics.objectives-state-class.0002.all: To benefit from economies of scale / increase profit / market share

economics.ped-data.0017.b: Premium has many substitutes: price elastic (PED -3.04), so price cut raises total revenue; basic habit product price inelastic, so raise price to increase revenue.
economics.ped-data.0017.c: Cut premium price: elastic, revenue rises (as shown); but costs/profit, competitor reaction. Basic: inelastic, cut reduces revenue; better raise price. Conclusion: do not cut both - only premium.

economics.pes-analyse-1.0007.all: Textiles: spare capacity, can raise output quickly, so PES elastic. Cotton: harvested once a year, long growing time, cannot raise output quickly in short run, so inelastic; perishable/storage issues.

economics.pes-assess-1.0006.all: Textiles react faster due to spare capacity, stocks; cotton constrained by annual harvest; but textiles need cotton input - shortage limits; cotton stockpiles allow some response; in long run cotton can expand planting. Judgement: mostly true, especially short run.

economics.pes-diagram.0017.all: Draw shallow (elastic) supply curve; mark P1 and P2 on price axis; read off Q1 and Q2 showing proportionally larger rise in quantity supplied (movement along curve).

economics.pes-explain.0002.all: Spare capacity (30% unused) means it can increase output quickly when price rises without large extra cost; so quantity supplied responds more than proportionately - PES > 1.

economics.price-data.0006.b: Poor harvests shift supply left; growing demand shifts demand right; both raise price; quantity effect uncertain; consumers may switch to substitutes.
economics.price-data.0006.c: Stay high: demand growth persistent, inelastic supply (olive trees slow to grow), climate change. Fall: harvests recover, supply shifts right, high prices encourage new planting, substitutes. Judgement depends on weather.

economics.price-diagram.0003.all: Demand shifts right D1; new equilibrium price P1 higher, quantity Q1 higher, labelled.

economics.production-analyse-2.0008.all: Value added by processing coffee - higher export revenue, improved current account; jobs and higher incomes; skills, FDI; less reliance on raw commodity price volatility; growth and multiplier.

economics.production-define2.0006.all: The decline in the importance of the secondary/manufacturing sector in an economy, measured by its share of output or employment.

economics.productivity-define2.0003.all: Splitting production into separate tasks, with each worker specialising in one task.

economics.protection-data.0006.b: Domestic producers face less competition from cheap/dumped imports, raise output, jobs, profits; protect against dumping; improve current account.
economics.protection-data.0006.c: Benefits: jobs, anti-dumping, industry. Costs: higher prices for consumers/firms using tyres, less choice, inefficiency, retaliation. Judgement depends on extent of dumping, duration.

economics.supply-analyse-1.0007.all: Drought reduces yields - supply shifts left; fertiliser price rise raises costs - supply shifts left; irrigation subsidy lowers costs/raises future yields - supply shifts right; net likely fall this year.

economics.supply-analyse-2.0002.all: Automation lowers unit costs/raises productivity - supply shifts right; 8% wage rise raises costs - supply left; tax on electronics raises costs - supply left; net effect depends on relative size.

economics.supply-diagram.0015.all: Supply shifts right to S1; new lower price P1 and higher quantity Q1 labelled.

economics.supply-explain.0013.all: Disease reduces cocoa yield/output; supply falls, shifting supply curve left; at each price less supplied, raising price.

economics.trade-state-class.0003.all: Domestic industries may close leading to unemployment

economics.unemployment-data.0011.b: Lower incomes and spending, multiplier reduces AD and growth; lower tax revenue, higher benefit spending - budget deficit; poverty, skills loss; hits construction and retail.
economics.unemployment-data.0011.c: For: raises AD via multiplier, infrastructure helps construction; counters cyclical unemployment. Against: budget deficit/debt, time lags, crowding out, may not fix structural unemployment. Judgement: yes for cyclical recession if finance available.

economics.protection-data.0006.problem: Part (a) wording glitch: "93,000 tyres of tyres a year" (and "tyres imports" in (c)); maths and MS otherwise correct (-29.03%).
economics.protection-data.0006.fix: "Before the quota, Rendova imported 93,000 tyres a year." and "the quota on tyre imports".
